Bootstrapping: learn before the reward arrives

How Monte Carlo, TD and n-step returns move credit backward, with a worked eight-state corridor.

The first seven moves give you no reward, and the eighth gives you one. How can the first move learn about that last reward before another walk begins? We can wait for the completed return or borrow an estimate of the next state's value. That borrowing is called bootstrapping. Let's compare these approaches in an eight-state corridor and follow how far each update carries credit. This makes the timing in Sutton and Barto, Chapters 5–7 explicit.

Part 2. Previously: the Q table.

Reading goal: compare one completed-return pass with eight forward TD walks and three walks of three-step TD in the same eight-state corridor. We'll keep the update order explicit throughout.

A late rewardWait for the returnBorrow the next estimateCredit travels backwardLook several steps aheadChoose the horizon

A late reward

Suppose you walk through eight states and receive 1 only when you leave the last one. Every earlier move earns zero, but each still leads toward that reward. We want the value of a state to account for the whole future after it, rather than just the next reward.

Let ttt be the current step, StS_tSt​ its state, AtA_tAt​ the action taken there, and Rt+1R_{t+1}Rt+1​ the reward after that action. The episode ends at step TTT. The discount γ\gammaγ, between 0 and 1 inclusive, reduces the weight of delayed rewards, and kkk counts steps ahead. The summation sign ∑\sum∑ adds the terms indexed by kkk, while γk\gamma^kγk discounts the reward at index kkk. Adding these discounted rewards gives us the return GtG_tGt​:

Gt=∑k=0T−t−1γkRt+k+1.G_t=\sum_{k=0}^{T-t-1}\gamma^k R_{t+k+1}. Gt​=k=0∑T−t−1​γkRt+k+1​.

A fixed policy π\piπ chooses the actions. Its true value vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s) at state sss is the expected return. Here Eπ\mathbb E_\piEπ​ means averaging over futures that follow that policy, and the vertical bar means conditioning on the starting state:

vπ(s)=Eπ[Gt∣St=s].v_\pi(s)=\mathbb E_\pi[G_t\mid S_t=s]. vπ​(s)=Eπ​[Gt​∣St​=s].

With no discounting, every nonterminal state in this deterministic corridor is worth 1. Those eight values connect the last reward to the earlier choices. Sutton and Barto, Chapter 3.

Wait for the return

The first seven rewards are zero, so none on its own explains why the first state is valuable. We can finish the walk and add up the rewards that followed each state. This is episodic Monte Carlo prediction. Let V(s)V(s)V(s) be our current estimate of vπ(s)v_\pi(s)vπ​(s), and let α\alphaα be a step size greater than zero and at most 1. The arrow ←\leftarrow← means we replace the estimate, and the brackets contain the error: the target minus the current estimate. For each state we visited, we move its estimate toward its completed return:

V(St)←V(St)+α[Gt−V(St)].V(S_t)\leftarrow V(S_t)+\alpha[G_t-V(S_t)]. V(St​)←V(St​)+α[Gt​−V(St​)].

Averaging sampled returns estimates the expected return. With a fixed policy, finite-variance returns, sufficient visits and suitable shrinking step sizes, the estimate settles toward that expectation. The target uses observed rewards throughout. Sutton and Barto, Section 5.1.

Follow the fixed policy until the episode ends.
Walk backward through the saved transitions.
Accumulate the discounted return.
Move each visited state's estimate toward its return.

In our corridor, let's start every estimate at zero and set both the step size and the discount to 1. After one completed walk, every state's target is 1, so every estimate becomes 1. Waiting works particularly well here because nothing is random: each return is exact.

The cost is having to wait. If an episode lasts a million steps, we can't make the first completed-return update until it ends. In a continuing task, there's no terminal event to give us this particular target.

The same problem shows up when a policy might never finish. In the windy gridworld of Sutton and Barto, Example 6.5, some policies never reach the goal, so Monte Carlo methods can't easily be used, while Sarsa learns during the episode that those policies are poor. Stopping the walk at a time limit does give us a number, but it's a truncated return: it leaves out whatever would have come next. Time limits below look at what that does to the targets.

Borrow the next estimate

What if the walk is still running? The return splits into the next reward and the return after it:

Gt=Rt+1+γGt+1.G_t=R_{t+1}+\gamma G_{t+1}. Gt​=Rt+1​+γGt+1​.

TD(0), one-step temporal-difference prediction, replaces the remaining return with our current estimate of the next state's value. In the equation above, Gt+1G_{t+1}Gt+1​ is the return from that next state. We'll call the resulting target YtY_tYt​ and its difference from the current estimate δt\delta_tδt​. This gives us the one-step backup used by TD(0):

Yt=Rt+1+γV(St+1),δt=Yt−V(St),V(St)←V(St)+αδt.\begin{aligned} Y_t&=R_{t+1}+\gamma V(S_{t+1}),\\ \delta_t&=Y_t-V(S_t),\\ V(S_t)&\leftarrow V(S_t)+\alpha\delta_t. \end{aligned} Yt​δt​V(St​)​=Rt+1​+γV(St+1​),=Yt​−V(St​),←V(St​)+αδt​.​

Set the terminal state's value to zero. The Bellman equation connects a state's expected return to its successor's expected return, and TD learns that relationship from sampled transitions. For a finite discounted continuing task, or a proper episodic task with bounded expected episode lengths, suitable on-policy visits and step sizes give convergence in the tabular case. Sutton and Barto, Sections 6.1–6.2.

Take one action from the fixed policy.
Observe its reward and next state.
Target = reward + discounted next-state estimate.
Move the current estimate toward that target.

Suppose the reward is 0, the discount is 0.9, and the next state's estimate is 0.8. With a current estimate of 0.2 and a step size of 0.5, the target is 0.72 and the error is 0.52, so the new estimate is 0.46. The reward stayed zero. The new information came from the successor's value.

Credit travels backward

Starting updates immediately doesn't mean new credit moves quickly. Let's return to the eight-state corridor, with zero initial estimates and α=γ=1\alpha=\gamma=1α=γ=1. We update online in forward order, once per visit, immediately after each transition.

On the first walk, the first seven targets are zero. Only the last state sees reward 1. On the second walk, state 7 reads the now-correct value at state 8. State 6 already updated before that happened, so it waits another walk.

After a complete walk States with value 1 under forward TD(0)
1 8
2 7, 8
3 6, 7, 8
8 1 through 8

We can write the same pattern as a formula without introducing another learning rule.

Let mmm count completed walks and iii identify a corridor state, from 1 to 8. Then Vm(i)V_m(i)Vm​(i) is that state's estimate after walk mmm, with m=0m=0m=0 meaning before learning begins. The cases below give the last mmm states a value of 1 and all the others a value of 0:

Vm(i)={1,i>8−m,0,i≤8−m,0≤m≤8.V_m(i)=\begin{cases}1,&i>8-m,\\0,&i\leq8-m,\end{cases}\qquad 0\leq m\leq8. Vm​(i)={1,0,​i>8−m,i≤8−m,​0≤m≤8.

On each forward pass, we read the next state's value before updating that next state. So credit moves backward by one state per walk. Monte Carlo credits all eight states after walk 1, while TD(0) needs eight walks to credit the first state.

These counts depend on the update order we chose. If we replayed the transitions backward, the reward would propagate across the whole chain in one pass. The corridor shows how information moves through these updates, but it doesn't tell us which method is faster in general.

Look several steps ahead

With forward one-step updates, credit moves back just one state per walk in our corridor. An n-step return follows several transitions before borrowing an estimate. Let nnn be the number of real rewards we want to use and h=min⁡(n,T−t)h=\min(n,T-t)h=min(n,T−t) the number available before the episode ends, where min⁡\minmin picks the smaller count. Call the resulting target Yt(n)Y_t^{(n)}Yt(n)​, with the superscript indicating the backup length, and its endpoint state St+hS_{t+h}St+h​:

Yt(n)=∑k=0h−1γkRt+k+1+{γhV(St+h),t+h<T,0,t+h=T.\begin{aligned} Y_t^{(n)}&=\sum_{k=0}^{h-1}\gamma^kR_{t+k+1}\\ &\quad+\begin{cases} \gamma^hV(S_{t+h}),&t+h<T,\\ 0,&t+h=T. \end{cases} \end{aligned} Yt(n)​​=k=0∑h−1​γkRt+k+1​+{γhV(St+h​),0,​t+h<T,t+h=T.​​

Each time we expand the return recursion, we get more observed rewards before the part we still have to guess. If we reach the terminal state, there's no future left to guess. Sutton and Barto, Section 7.1.

Save transitions until n rewards are available.
Sum those rewards with their discounts.
Add the endpoint estimate if the episode continues.
Update the starting state; flush short returns at the end.

With three-step updates in the same corridor, the last three states receive credit on walk 1. The next three receive it on walk 2, and the first two on walk 3. This uses the usual delayed online n-step updates, followed by the terminal flush.

You wait longer for each target, but it can carry a newly observed outcome across more states. When the target reaches the end, it becomes the completed Monte Carlo return.

Choose the horizon

A longer target uses more actual experience and less of the current guess. In a task with randomness, it also includes more random rewards and transitions. For any state sss, let ε(s)=V(s)−vπ(s)\varepsilon(s)=V(s)-v_\pi(s)ε(s)=V(s)−vπ​(s) be the estimation error: approximate value minus true policy value. St+nS_{t+n}St+n​ is the endpoint after nnn real transitions. Before termination, the guessed tail's contribution to target error is

γnε(St+n).\gamma^n\varepsilon(S_{t+n}). γnε(St+n​).

The discount shrinks a given endpoint error as the horizon grows. But the endpoint itself changes with nnn, so this expression doesn't tell us that target bias or variance will always rise or fall with the horizon. Noisy rewards, correlated transitions and the accuracy of different endpoint estimates all matter. Sutton and Barto, Chapters 6–7.

Method Learns Target Fails when Adjustment Source
Monte Carlo Policy value Full return Episodes are too long Bootstrap sooner Ch. 5
TD(0) Policy value One reward + guess Credit moves slowly Extend backup Ch. 6
n-step TD Policy value Several rewards + guess Targets wait or fluctuate Tune horizon Ch. 7

In this corridor: Monte Carlo waits for 8 rewards and credits all states after walk 1. TD(0) starts after 1 reward but needs 8 forward walks to credit state 1. Three-step TD waits for up to 3 rewards and needs 3 walks. These counts hold for zero initialization and unit discount and step size. They don't establish a performance ranking in stochastic tasks.

Bootstrapping buys:

  • Early updates. Learn before an episode finishes.
  • Continuing prediction. Use discounted targets without waiting for an ending.
  • Shared successors. Reuse what other visits taught the next state's estimate.

Costs and assumptions:

  • Wrong targets. An inaccurate successor can mislead its predecessors.
  • State quality. Tabular prediction assumes states contain the information needed to predict transitions.
  • Coupled values. Shared parameters can move the target during learning; off-policy data adds another stability concern.

Give actions credit

So far, we've estimated values under a fixed policy. Suppose we now want to improve that policy. A good outcome alone doesn't tell us whether an action helped: perhaps the starting state was already promising. The advantage compares an action's expected return with the policy's usual return from that state:

Aπ(s,a)=Qπ(s,a)−Vπ(s).A_\pi(s,a)=Q_\pi(s,a)-V_\pi(s). Aπ​(s,a)=Qπ​(s,a)−Vπ​(s).

Here QπQ_\piQπ​ means taking aaa first and then following π\piπ. For VπV_\piVπ​, we also average over the first action chosen by the policy. Both are true policy values. Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) uses experience and an approximate state value VVV to estimate this action credit.

Collect a rollout with a fixed policy, then keep both the data and VVV fixed while calculating advantages. Take one segment ending at SHS_HSH​, with HHH transitions, and let ℓ\ellℓ count steps ahead. Using the same reward convention as before, the one-step TD error and finite GAE estimate are

δt=Rt+1+γV(St+1)−V(St),A^t=∑ℓ=0H−t−1(γλ)ℓδt+ℓ.\begin{aligned} \delta_t&=R_{t+1}+\gamma V(S_{t+1})-V(S_t),\\ \hat A_t&=\sum_{\ell=0}^{H-t-1}(\gamma\lambda)^\ell\delta_{t+\ell}. \end{aligned} δt​A^t​​=Rt+1​+γV(St+1​)−V(St​),=ℓ=0∑H−t−1​(γλ)ℓδt+ℓ​.​

The parameter λ\lambdaλ, between 0 and 1, controls how much later errors contribute. To connect this sum to the returns we've already used, take one return length and add its TD errors with powers of γ\gammaγ. The intermediate value estimates cancel, leaving a return estimate minus the starting value. GAE can also be written as a geometrically weighted mixture of these estimates across different return lengths, with the remaining weight on the longest available return. Schulman et al., Section 3, equations 14–16.

This brings the same horizon tradeoff to action credit. Shorter returns depend more on a guessed tail that may be biased, while longer returns include more observed rewards and transitions that can add noise. GAE mixes return lengths rather than picking just one. Its bias and variance still depend on how accurate the values are and on the task, so changing λ\lambdaλ doesn't guarantee a particular change in variance.

Let's take a small example with three transitions ending at a terminal state. Set γ=1\gamma=1γ=1, with rewards (R1,R2,R3)=(0,0,4)(R_1,R_2,R_3)=(0,0,4)(R1​,R2​,R3​)=(0,0,4) and frozen values (V(S0),V(S1),V(S2),V(S3))=(2,2,1,0)(V(S_0),V(S_1),V(S_2),V(S_3))=(2,2,1,0)(V(S0​),V(S1​),V(S2​),V(S3​))=(2,2,1,0). This gives errors of (0,−1,3)(0,-1,3)(0,−1,3). With λ=0.5\lambda=0.5λ=0.5, each later error gets half the weight of the previous one when we calculate credit for action A0A_0A0​:

The same sum has a short backward recurrence:

A^H=0,A^t=δt+γλA^t+1.\hat A_H=0,\qquad \hat A_t=\delta_t+\gamma\lambda\hat A_{t+1}. A^H​=0,A^t​=δt​+γλA^t+1​.

To apply this recurrence to a batch, split it at every episode reset. For each segment, use the last actual observation as SHS_HSH​. Set V(SH)=0V(S_H)=0V(SH​)=0 only at a true terminal state. A time limit that truncates an ongoing task, or a rollout cutoff, keeps its bootstrap value; the trace still stops at the boundary. This matches the boundary handling in Spinning Up's finish_path.

# One segment, with frozen values and no episode reset inside it.
endpoint = 0 if true_terminal else V(last_actual_observation)
v[H] = endpoint
advantage[H] = 0
for t = H-1 down to 0:
    delta = R_(t+1) + gamma * v[t+1] - v[t]
    advantage[t] = delta + gamma * lambda * advantage[t+1]

Here v[t] stores the frozen V(St)V(S_t)V(St​). At λ=1\lambda=1λ=1, cancellation gives

A^t=∑ℓ=0H−t−1γℓRt+ℓ+1+γH−tV(SH)−V(St).\hat A_t=\sum_{\ell=0}^{H-t-1}\gamma^\ell R_{t+\ell+1}+\gamma^{H-t}V(S_H)-V(S_t). A^t​=ℓ=0∑H−t−1​γℓRt+ℓ+1​+γH−tV(SH​)−V(St​).

Only a true terminal endpoint removes that tail. A truncated return still includes it.

When the clock ends the episode

That rule assumes we know whether an ending is real. Training runs usually stop every episode after a fixed number of steps, and that cutoff can mean two different things. Pardo et al. (2018) separate them.

The time limit is part of the task. Say the robot really has 14 moves to reach a goal. Then the value of a state depends on how many moves are left: the same square is worth a lot with 10 moves left and nothing with 1 move left if the goal is 3 moves away. If the state doesn't include the remaining time, those two situations look identical, and the learner averages targets that disagree. Their fix is to put the remaining time in the input.

Their Last Moment example shows how much this matters. At each step the agent can stay, for reward 0, or jump into a trap that gives +1 once and then −1 on every step until the episode ends. The best plan is to stay and jump on the very last step, collecting +1 with no penalty. An agent that can't see the clock can't tell when the last step is. With more than two steps in the episode, its best fixed choice is to never jump, and the paper notes that even Monte Carlo methods, which don't bootstrap, can't learn the right plan without the time input.

The time limit is only for training. If the task would really go on, the cutoff isn't an end. Treating it as terminal teaches the learner that a state near the cutoff is worth less, even though nothing about that state changed. Their fix is partial-episode bootstrapping: at the cutoff, use R+γV(S′)R+\gamma V(S')R+γV(S′) instead of RRR, which is the truncation rule from the GAE section.

How the limit is meant Value depends on Target at the limit Fix from Pardo et al.
Part of the task State and time left Real end: last reward only Add the remaining time to the input
Only for training State only Not an end: bootstrap from V(S′)V(S')V(S′) Partial-episode bootstrapping

So the right handling depends on the objective. Bootstrapping through a limit that's really part of the task is also a mistake: it assumes a future that the task doesn't have.

My game Breaking Bellman has a pass-or-fail goal grid where this seems to happen: 14 moves, reward 1 at the goal and 0 otherwise, no discount. PPO with a learned value and GAE solved 13.3% of the tasks, and its value estimate at the start was about 1.44, above the largest possible return of 1. Scoring actions with real completed returns instead solved 95%, and with no baseline at all, 100% (3 seeds, simulation). The game's own reading is that the value bootstraps through the time limit and can't see the clock. That fits the first case, but the log has no run with the remaining time in the input that would confirm it.

The next question is how to store values when almost every state is new. Part 3: function approximation replaces separate table entries with shared weights.
